summary: Barnard's Star is a known red dwarf about 6.0 light-years away, with a Gaia temperature estimate of 3,100 K. It is the fastest-moving star in our sky. WANDERERS measured a 164-arcsecond shift between 2010 and 2026. That is 10.39 arcseconds per year, within 0.1% of the Gaia value, so our confidence is high. The star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 150 measurements are flagged and we show no spectrum. Its brightness change, -0.04 ± 0.03 mag, is uncertain because the star's core is saturated.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Three checks agree. The star moved 164 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026. That is about 10.39 arcseconds per year, within 0.1% of the Gaia DR3 catalogue speed. Gaia DR3 also lists this star, at about 6.0 light-years. One caution: the star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 150 measurements are flagged. The brightness change of -0.04 ± 0.03 mag comes only from the faint edges of the star's image.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: A few things would shake my confidence. The total speed matches Gaia almost exactly, but the east-west part is a little off: we measured -777 and Gaia says -802 milliarcseconds per year. A bigger gap there would worry me. The star is too bright for SPHEREx, so all 150 spectrum points are flagged. The brightness check also uses only the star's outer glow. That -0.04 ± 0.03 mag change is too small and too uncertain to trust.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: The two telescopes give two snapshots far apart in time. WISE pictured this patch of sky around 2010, and SPHEREx pictured it again in 2026. Over about 16 years, Barnard's Star moved 164 arcseconds, or 26.6 SPHEREx pixels. That long gap makes its speed easy to measure: 10.39 arcseconds per year, which matches Gaia. All 150 SPHEREx measurements are flagged because the star is too bright.
